paras: The Sandy Ridge posse fight was an armed clash on May 4, 1888, in Lowndes County, Alabama, between a sheriff's posse making arrests and a group of armed Black men. Two or three deputies were wounded, and the governor sent state troops; reports of Black casualties ranged from "several negroes killed" to none hurt. Days later a dispatch said a wounded man, Emerson Shepherd, had died after swearing to a plot to massacre whites.

In March 1888 Theo Calloway, a Black man accused of killing a white man named Mitchell Gresham near Sandy Ridge, was lynched at Hayneville, the county seat; one dispatch said he had claimed self-defense. May dispatches traced the new trouble to that lynching, saying Black residents had been "threatening vengeance" ever since. A news brief added that the sheriff, asked by the governor for an account of the lynching, "replied practically that his excellency might mind his own business."

By the fuller wire version, whites around Sandy Ridge sought the sheriff's protection and twenty warrants were sworn out against Black men. A telegram from Fort Deposit instead said the grand jury had indicted about thirteen; neither account states the charges. Days earlier the sheriff had wounded a man resisting arrest, which, by the Montgomery account, "infuriated the negroes, and precipitated the conflict."

On May 4 the sheriff, named in one dispatch as Brinson, and a posse that one account put at fifty armed white men arrested about fifteen Black men at Sandy Ridge. Returning toward Hayneville, the posse met what the wire called "a mob of armed negroes," 150 mounted men by one report. The men "showed fight" when summoned to surrender, by the Fort Deposit account, and after several volleys dispersed. Deputy sheriffs Rice, Meriwether and D. Cook were reported wounded.

That evening Governor Seay referred a telegram from citizens asking for troops to section 4,703 of the state code; when the sheriff telegraphed for troops "to repress mob violence," he sent Col. Thomas G. Jones with the Montgomery Grays, Blues and Mounted Rifles. The troops marched about twenty miles to Sandy Ridge, helped make arrests, and returned on May 5.

Arrests continued: twenty-four "ringleaders" were jailed at Hayneville by May 5, forty-one by May 6, and forty-eight by later reports. The same day two men, Kit Webb and "Shack" Means, were reported fatally wounded and hidden in the swamps, and Bob Meriwether wounded.

On May 9 a dispatch datelined St. Louis, crediting "several reliable gentlemen," printed a sworn statement attributed to Emerson Shepherd, "fatally shot in the fight with the sheriff's posse," who "has since died." In it Shepherd described lodges raising money for ammunition "to kill the whites if they attempted to arrest the negroes," naming Bob Robinson and Neal Mangum as leaders. No report of an inquest or a trial appears in the coverage.

The May 5 wire reports ran under headlines such as "Uprising in Alabama," "A Race War in Alabama" and "A Pitched Battle." The Memphis Appeal warned that Black residents outnumbered whites "fully ten to one." Savannah's Morning News later headed the report of wounded Black men "Dying in the Swamps" over "The Lowndes County Rioters Paying for Their Lawlessness."

The Shepherd statement ran from May 9 to May 16 under headings such as "A Plot to Murder the Whites" and "They Are Banded to Kill." Some papers doubted the story: the Helena Weekly Herald headed it "Another of those Alleged Massacres that Never Come to Pass," and the Sauk Centre Herald called the affair "the same old story." The sharpest dissent came from the Oskaloosa Herald in Iowa, whose editorial "The Usual Treatment" mocked the "noble Caucassian" and charged that the Associated Press was "controlled wholly in the interest of the making assassination respectable."

Casualty reports ranged from "several negroes killed" in the first wire to two "probably killed" in a later dispatch. The dispatch on the troops' return said "It is not known that any negroes were hurt," and on May 6 the Morning News reported two fatally wounded but "None of the negroes are dead." Shepherd's death rests on the second-hand St. Louis dispatch, which also dated the fight "last Thursday evening" rather than Friday, May 4.

reader.title: Sandy Ridge posse fight
bases: A sheriff's posse serving warrants clashed with armed Black men on the road from Sandy Ridge to Hayneville, wounding several and reportedly killing one or more, though deaths are disputed (A2, A6, A14, A19).

The shooting was done by a sheriff's posse of up to fifty men making arrests on warrants or indictments, i.e. under color of law, in an exchange of volleys with armed men (A32, A5, A2); whether anyone died is contested (A14, A17, A19).

Many papers agree on the clash and the wounded deputies (A2, A6, A5), but reports of Black deaths run from 'several' killed to 'not known that any negroes were hurt' and 'None of the negroes are dead' (A2, A14, A17).

accounts.label: Montgomery wire (Advertiser special)
accounts.gist: The posse, returning with fifteen prisoners, 'encountered a mob of armed negroes'; two whites wounded and several Black men killed before the Black group dispersed.

accounts.label: Fort Deposit telegram
accounts.gist: Men indicted by the grand jury 'showed fight' when summoned to surrender and were reinforced; several whites slightly wounded, a number of Black men reported killed and wounded.

accounts.label: Troops-returned dispatch
accounts.gist: Two deputies shot and doing well; 'It is not known that any negroes were hurt'; trouble blamed on resistance to arrest.

accounts.label: May 6 Montgomery dispatch
accounts.gist: Two Black men fatally wounded in the swamps, one more wounded, none yet dead; five ringleaders surrendered.

accounts.label: Shepherd statement (relayed via St. Louis)
accounts.gist: A dying man's sworn statement, reported second hand, that lodges had planned to massacre whites and to resist arrests with arms.

accounts.label: Oskaloosa Herald editorial
accounts.gist: The Black men had protested lynchings and the whites, with Associated Press help, turned it into a pretext for troops and 'legal slaughter'.

framing.detail: May 5 wire headlines: 'Uprising in Alabama', 'A Race War in Alabama', 'A Pitched Battle', 'Riot in Alabama'; Black men called 'a mob of armed negroes'.
Savannah Morning News: 'Dying in the Swamps. The Lowndes County Rioters Paying for Their Lawlessness'; Memphis Appeal said prisoners 'were bent on a wholesale destruction of human life'.
Plot story headed 'A Plot to Murder the Whites', 'They Are Banded to Kill', 'A Massacre Planned'.
Helena Weekly Herald ran the plot story under 'Another of those Alleged Massacres that Never Come to Pass'; Sauk Centre Herald: 'the same old story ... Of course!'
Oskaloosa Herald editorial 'The Usual Treatment' attacked the white mob, the Associated Press and Alabama's treatment of Black men.
